findings.who: A filer or spouse who paid 2025 interest on a general-purpose loan, such as a bank personal loan or a loan from a non-related individual, that was taken out solely to pay college tuition, fees, room and board. The lender called it a personal loan and sent no Form 1098-E.
findings.why_no: "Paid interest on a student loan" reads as a loan labeled or marketed as a student loan, such as a federal Direct, PLUS or private education loan. A borrower whose loan paperwork says personal loan answers no, and nothing in the gate tells them the label does not matter.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 98, Qualified student loan: "A qualified student loan is any loan you took out to pay the qualified higher education expenses for any of the following individuals who were eligible students."
findings.fix: Ask: "In 2025, did you (or your spouse) pay interest on any loan taken out to pay college or vocational school costs (tuition, fees, room and board, books) for you, your spouse or a dependent? Count it even if the lender didn't call it a student loan or send a Form 1098-E." Sort out non-qualifying loans afterward with sli.unqualified_any.

findings.who: A former student, not claimable as anyone's dependent, whose parent or other relative made the 2025 payments on the student's own qualified student loan as a gift.
findings.why_no: "You (or your spouse) paid interest" is literally false, because the parent paid. Yet the IRS treats a payment someone else makes on your behalf as paid by you when you aren't a dependent. The gate's words and help give no hint of this.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 98, Line 21: "You paid interest in 2025 on a qualified student loan". Pub. 970 (not in the snapshots above) treats interest paid on your behalf by another person as paid by you if you are not claimed as a dependent.
findings.fix: Add help: "Count interest someone else (such as a parent) paid on your loan as paid by you, unless someone can claim you as a dependent. Don't count payments your employer or a loan repayment program made; those are asked about next."

findings.who: A borrower whose 2025 payments partly covered interest that had accrued and been capitalized during school or deferment. The loan servicer reports little or nothing in box 1 of Form 1098-E, or sends no form.
findings.why_no: The filer sees only principal reduction on the statement and no reported interest, so they treat the payments as principal. They answer no to having paid interest.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 99, Student Loan Interest Deduction Worksheet line 1: "Enter the total interest you paid in 2025 on qualified student loans"
findings.fix: Add help: "Payments can include interest that was added to the loan balance earlier (capitalized interest). If you made any payment on a student loan in 2025, answer yes and check the lender's statement."

findings.who: A physician or nurse in the NHSC Loan Repayment Program, or a qualifying state health-professional loan repayment program, gets the repayment money in their own account. They then pay their loan servicer, interest included, from that account.
findings.why_no: The helper asks whether interest was 'paid ... through tax-free student loan repayment assistance'. The filer made every payment personally, so they read the payments as their own, not as made through the program.
findings.irs_text: p4681 p. 5: 'Student loan repayments made to you are tax free if you received them for ... The National Health Service Corps (NHSC) Loan Repayment Program' and 'You can't deduct the interest you paid on a student loan to the extent payments were made through your participation in any of the above programs.'
findings.fix: Ask by fact, not by payment route: 'Did you (or your spouse) receive money in 2025, paid to you or to your lender, from the National Health Service Corps Loan Repayment Program, a state education loan repayment program under the Public Health Service Act, or another state loan repayment or forgiveness program for health services in underserved or shortage areas?' Then ask how much of the interest those funds covered.

findings.who: A health professional in a state rural or underserved-area loan repayment program who doesn't know whether the program's payments are excluded from income. The program may name itself without mentioning health shortage areas, or the filer may assume all forgiveness is taxable.
findings.why_no: The word 'tax-free' makes the filer classify the program. A filer who believes or guesses the assistance is taxable, or who doesn't see it described as tax-free, answers no.
findings.irs_text: p4681 p. 5: 'Any other state loan repayment or loan forgiveness program that is intended to provide for the increased availability of health services in underserved or health professional shortage areas (as determined by such state).'
findings.fix: Drop 'tax-free' from the filer-facing question. Ask whether any student loan payments were made by or through a loan repayment or forgiveness program, naming the NHSC and state health-service programs. Have the tool or the help text decide which programs qualify.

findings.who: A student-borrower whose parent or grandparent owns a 529 plan, and the owner took a distribution and paid part of the borrower's 2025 student loan interest with it. The borrower took no distribution of their own.
findings.why_no: The borrower doesn't think of the payment as theirs: 'my parents' 529 paid it, I didn't take a distribution.' They read the question as asking about their own plan or their own payment.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 98, line 21: 'Don't include any amount paid from a distribution of earnings made from a qualified tuition program (QTP) after 2018 to the extent the earnings are treated as tax free because they were used to pay student loan interest.'
findings.fix: Say 'from any 529 plan or other qualified tuition program, whoever owns the account (for example, a parent's plan)'. Add help text saying that payments made for you count.

findings.who: A filer who took a 529 distribution, reported on Form 1099-Q, to pay down student loans. They know the distribution came from the plan but think of it as the money in their account, not as 'earnings'.
findings.why_no: 'Paid from tax-free qualified tuition program earnings' reads like a narrow investment-gains concept. A filer who sees 'distribution' or 'withdrawal' on their 1099-Q, not 'earnings', or who thinks they used contributions, answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 98, line 21: 'Don't include any amount paid from a distribution of earnings made from a qualified tuition program (QTP) after 2018 to the extent the earnings are treated as tax free because they were used to pay student loan interest.'
findings.fix: Ask broadly first: 'Was any of the student loan interest paid with money withdrawn from a 529 plan or other qualified tuition program (Form 1099-Q)?' Then work out the earnings share from the 1099-Q basis and earnings boxes, or ask for it.

findings.who: A loan repayment program participant whose program money for 2025 interest arrives in a different year. For example, they paid interest during 2025 and the program reimbursed them in early 2026, or a lump sum received in 2024 was applied to 2025 payments.
findings.why_no: The filer links 'paid ... through assistance' to when the assistance arrived. They see no assistance received in 2025 that matches their 2025 payments, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: p4681 p. 5: 'You can't deduct the interest you paid on a student loan to the extent payments were made through your participation in any of the above programs.'
findings.fix: Make the question about the 2025 interest payments however funded, for example: 'Was any of the interest you paid in 2025 funded by such a program, whether the program paid you before or after you paid the loan?'

findings.who: A joint filer whose spouse's student loan interest was paid partly through NHSC assistance or the spouse's 529 distribution. The filer answering knows only their own loan.
findings.why_no: The parent helper says 'You (or, on a joint return, your spouse)', but the child helper says only 'Any of that interest'. A filer who answers about their own loan says no.
findings.irs_text: p4681 p. 5: 'You can't deduct the interest you paid on a student loan to the extent payments were made through your participation in any of the above programs.'
findings.fix: Repeat the spouse in the child question: 'Was any of the interest you or your spouse paid ...'

findings.who: A parent pays the interest on a loan their child took out for the child's own tuition. The parent is not the borrower and is not legally obligated on the loan. The child has a Form 1098-E with the parent's payments on it.
findings.why_no: The loan is a federal student loan used only for tuition, so the parent truthfully says it is a qualified student loan. The gate never asks whose loan it is. The definition 'any loan you took out' makes it not qualified for the payer.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 98: 'A qualified student loan is any loan you took out to pay the qualified higher education expenses...'
findings.fix: Before the classification question, ask: 'Did you (or your spouse) take out the loan and are you legally obligated to pay it?' Treat interest you paid on someone else's loan as not on a qualified student loan.

findings.who: A borrower spent part of a private student loan's refunded excess on a car or rent beyond the cost of attendance. Or a borrower refinanced student loans together with credit-card debt or took cash out in the refinance.
findings.why_no: The lender calls it a student loan and sends Form 1098-E, so the filer reads 'not a qualified student loan' as not applying. The filer doesn't see that any non-education use of the proceeds disqualifies the whole loan.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 99: 'a loan isn't a qualified student loan if (a) any of the proceeds were used for other purposes'
findings.fix: Ask for the facts the filer can check: 'Was any part of the loan's money used for something other than tuition, fees, room and board, books, supplies and similar school costs? This includes a refinance or consolidation that included other debt or cash out.'

findings.who: A loan paid for a student who was not one of the listed people. Examples: a niece or a friend's child; the filer's own child who had gross income of $5,200 or more (the exemption amount) the year the loan was taken out; a person who filed a joint return; or a loan taken out while the filer could be claimed as someone else's dependent.
findings.why_no: The help names only (a) other-use proceeds and (b) related-person or employer-plan lenders. A filer reads those two as the whole rule and says no. The student-eligibility and dependency limits in the definition are not visible.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi pp. 98–99: 'for any of the following individuals who were eligible students. 1. Yourself or your spouse. 2. Any person who was your dependent when the loan was taken out. 3. Any person you could have claimed as a dependent ... except that: a. ... joint return; b. ... gross income ... $5,200 for 2025; or c. You ... could be claimed as a dependent'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Was every loan taken out only for yourself, your spouse, or someone who was your dependent (or could have been) when the loan was taken out?' Add follow-ups for the joint-return, gross-income and you-were-a-dependent exceptions.

findings.who: A parent's child is a dependent in 2025, but was not a dependent when the loan was taken out years earlier. For example, the child was independent then and had too much income.
findings.why_no: The filer applies today's dependency status instead of the status 'when the loan was taken out', and answers that the loan was for a dependent.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 99: 'Any person who was your dependent when the loan was taken out'; 'for the year the loan was taken out'
findings.fix: State the time frame in the question: 'when the loan was taken out (not in 2025)'.

findings.who: A student attended a program that was not an eligible educational institution, for example some foreign schools or a non-degree course. Or the student was not enrolled at least half-time in a degree, certificate or similar program. Or the loan paid for costs above the expenses net of scholarships.
findings.why_no: The filer sees 'student loan' and tuition use, and takes 'qualified higher education expenses' to mean any schooling costs.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 99: 'The expenses must be for education in a degree, certificate, or similar program at an eligible educational institution'; p. 98: 'individuals who were eligible students'
findings.fix: Add a fact question: 'Was the school a college, university or eligible vocational school, and was the student in a degree or certificate program?' Note in help that amounts beyond the cost of attendance net of scholarships disqualify the loan.

findings.who: A filer borrowed for tuition from a grandparent, a sibling, or a company controlled by the family, with written interest terms.
findings.why_no: 'Related person' is a legal term. The filer may think it means only a parent, or may not see a business entity as a related person.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 99: '(b) the loan was from either a related person or a person who borrowed the proceeds under a qualified employer plan'
findings.fix: Spell it out in help: a related person includes a spouse, siblings, parents, grandparents, children, grandchildren, and businesses controlled by family. Also mention loans the lender funded from a 401(k) or other plan loan.
